feedback: If a flat roof lets water pool and drip through, prompt: 'What could you change about the roof shape so the water runs off instead of sitting there?'
When a child reshapes the roof into a slope and the rain runs off, affirm: 'You changed the SHAPE and that solved it — can you say why the slope helps?'
If a tower on a narrow base topples, ask: 'What shape of base would stop it wobbling?' and let them widen it and re-test.
If labels only name the goal ('stays dry'), ask them to name the feature that achieves it ('the sloped roof sends rain off the edge').
activities.intendedInsight: It was not a fancier roof that kept the animals dry — it was the SHAPE: a slope sends water away, and a wide base helps keep a structure from tipping. Form does functional work, and a model lets you show and improve how a design works.
learnerActions: Read/hear the given problem: 'Design a shelter that keeps the toy animals DRY in the rain.'
Assemble a shelter from choosable parts — a base, walls, and a roof you can shape as flat, domed, or sloped — drawing or placing your solution.

Run a rain check: on a flat roof, watch whether water sits and pools (and, if the roof has gaps or leaks, drips through onto the animals); reshape the roof into a slope that overhangs the walls and run the rain again to see whether the water runs off the edge and away from the animals.
Try a stability challenge too: give a tall tower a narrow base, test it with a gentle nudge (it may wobble or topple), then widen the base and re-test to compare.
Label your finished design with why each shape helps, e.g. 'the roof is sloped so the rain runs off.'
activities.title: Shape Shop: build and test a shelter

feedback: If the child draws a decorative, detailed picture (colours, patterns, a happy bird) with no stopping mechanism, refocus: 'Which part actually stops the squirrel? Draw just that part big.' Value the working feature over decoration.
If the model doesn't connect to the problem, ask: 'What would a squirrel try, and what about your shape stops it there?' Build the link one feature at a time.
If the child labels a wish ('no squirrels here') with no physical feature, ask: 'What SHAPE makes that happen?' and replace the label with a feature.
Probe deeper: 'Why did you make that part that shape rather than round/flat/wider?' and 'A real squirrel can jump and hang upside down — does your shape still work? What would you change?'
activities.intendedInsight: A good model foregrounds the working feature and can be justified by how its shape solves the problem, and it adapts when the challenge gets harder — the model shows how a design works, not just what it looks like.
learnerActions: Take the problem: birds keep eating from the feeder, but so do the squirrels. Design a feeder birds can use but squirrels can't reach the food in.
On paper or with simple materials, sketch or build a quick model of your idea.
Point to the specific shape or structural feature that stops the squirrels (e.g. a narrow perch, a dome, or a baffle) and explain how that feature does the job.
Relate your model back to the real feeder and the real squirrels.
Raise the challenge: a squirrel can jump and hang upside down — does your shape still work? Change it and re-explain if needed.
activities.title: Design a squirrel-proof bird feeder (make-and-explain)

feedback: For a correct match, prompt the reason: 'Right — why does that shape win for this job?'
For an incorrect match, point back to the function: 'What does this part need to DO? Which shape helps with that?'
activities.intendedInsight: You can recognise which shapes suit which functions and give a shape-based reason for the match.
learnerActions: Look at pairs of shapes and the jobs they might do, and match each shape to the function it serves.
Given a problem, choose which of several shapes would best solve it (e.g. which roof would keep rain out).
Sort shapes into 'good for this job' and 'poor for this job' for a stated purpose, and say why.
activities.title: Match the shape to its job (check of understanding)
